title: The History of Streaming Music
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of streaming music, from the CD-era pricing frustrations and the rise of Napster and file sharing, through early streaming services (Launch Media, Rhapsody, Pandora with its Music Genome Project), the RIAA and Metallica lawsuits, Spotify's launch and royalty model, the Tidal launch with artist ownership, Neil Young's Pono player, Apple Music, and today's per-stream royalty economics and the Living Wage for Musicians Act. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about a kid named Boden from a Minecraft episode.
topics: Copyright Royalty and Distribution Reform Act of 2004

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with a joke about streaming and introduce the topic of the history of streaming music, which Chuck suggested.

segments.title: CD prices and album frustrations
segments.summary: The hosts recall that CDs cost around nineteen ninety-nine and that albums often had only one or two good songs, leading listeners to feel burned and become willing to find music another way.

segments.title: Napster and the rise of file sharing
segments.summary: Sean Fanning and Sean Parker created Napster as a peer-to-peer file sharing service. CD ripping software let users build MP3 collections that could be traded. Napster grew to tens of millions of users within two years.

segments.title: Musicians, labels and the lawsuits
segments.summary: Some artists supported file sharing, such as Chuck D, while others opposed it. Metallica and Dr. Dre sued, and the RIAA sued individual users, including a twelve-year-old girl. Metallica had Napster ban users it identified.

segments.title: Napster's decline and its successors
segments.summary: Napster's publicity drew more users. It tried to become a legitimate service, paying royalties and offering subscriptions, but competitors such as LimeWire, Kazaa and FrostWire had arrived and it did not succeed as a business.

segments.title: iTunes, the 99-cent song and the decline of physical sales
segments.summary: Apple's iTunes launched in 2003 selling songs for 99 cents. Hosts discuss how labels could have priced CDs lower and cite statistics showing physical sales fell sixty percent between 2001 and 2010.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next segment.

segments.title: Early streaming services: Launch Media and Rhapsody
segments.summary: Early streaming services like Launch Media played radio-style programming with limited skipping, and the RIAA objected to skipping. Rhapsody launched in 2001 as the first legitimate on-demand service and was later rebranded as Napster in 2016. Real Player was used for streaming.

segments.title: Columbia House story
segments.summary: Josh recounts his Columbia House record club experience at age twelve, where he sent back unwanted albums with a letter saying minors cannot enter contracts, and the company stopped sending them.

segments.title: Pandora and the Music Genome Project
segments.summary: Pandora launched in 2005 as Savage Beast Technologies and recommended music using the Music Genome Project, which analyzed about 450 attributes of each song. Pandora tried a three-dollar subscription with a free trial, but conversion was low, partly because people were wary of entering credit card information online.

segments.title: Copyright Royalty Board and the 2004 Act
segments.summary: Congress passed the Copyright Royalty and Distribution Reform Act of 2004, creating the US Copyright Royalty Board to settle royalty disputes between streamers and labels. The legal complexity hurt smaller streaming companies, including Yahoo Music, which shut down.
topics: Copyright Royalty and Distribution Reform Act

segments.title: iPhone and mobile streaming
segments.summary: The iPhone in 2007 let users play downloaded and streamed music on a phone. The Pandora iPhone app quickly reached about a quarter of iPhones. Chuck and Josh reminisce about app-focused meetings at their TV show.

segments.title: Spotify's launch and royalty model
segments.summary: Spotify launched in Stockholm in 2006 and reached the US in 2011. It paid roughly 70 percent of revenue as royalties and lost money for years before its first profitable quarters in 2024, reportedly through layoffs and subscription price increases.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before the Tidal discussion.

segments.title: Tidal launch and its troubles
segments.summary: Tidal launched in 2015 as an artist-owned service backed by Jay Z, with higher bitrates and human editors. Its launch event was awkward, and the company was sued for underpayment. Jack Dorsey's Block Inc. bought an 86 percent share for 300 million dollars in 2021, and a shareholder lawsuit against Dorsey was dismissed.

segments.title: Neil Young's Pono player and audio quality
segments.summary: Neil Young's crowdfunded Pono player, launched in 2015, argued MP3s were poor quality. The hosts explain bitrates and note that most listeners cannot detect differences above about 256 kbps, compared with about 1,400 kbps for CDs.

segments.title: Apple Music and Steve Jobs' objections
segments.summary: Apple Music launched in 2015, late to streaming, reportedly because Steve Jobs opposed subscription rental of music. Amazon also launched a streaming service about a year later. Jobs' argument about renting versus owning is discussed.

segments.title: Streaming revenue recovery and artist payouts
segments.summary: Music industry revenue fell to a low around 2014 and recovered by 2022. Subscriptions make up most revenue. Per-stream rates differ by service: Tidal about 1.3 cents, Apple and YouTube Music about 0.7 cents, Spotify and Amazon 0.4 cents, Pandora 0.1 cents. Spotify paid over nine billion dollars in 2023, and many independent artists earn significant income.

segments.title: Viral songs, most-streamed artists and changing songwriting
segments.summary: Pavement's 1996 B-side Harness Your Hopes went viral on TikTok and reached about 148 million Spotify streams. The Weeknd's Blinding Lights is cited as the most streamed song on Spotify. Record labels reportedly request short viral hooks, and the album era is described as declining.

segments.title: Living Wage for Musicians Act
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the proposed Living Wage for Musicians Act, which would set a minimum royalty of one cent per stream, and mention an online petition to sign.

segments.title: Genre experimentation and closing banter
segments.summary: Hosts argue that streaming lets artists take creative risks, then joke about forming a band. Jerry, the producer, is mentioned for slide whistle.

segments.title: Listener mail: Boden correction
segments.summary: Sarah writes to correct an earlier omission from the Minecraft episode, identifying her son Boden as the kid at the Medford show who asked about Minecraft.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to suggest episodes by email and close with the show credit.
